nameStory: This grasshopper gets its name from its love of huckleberry patches, where it's commonly found munching on the low-growing shrubs. The name 'huckleberry' comes from the old English 'hurtleberry,' referring to the small, dark berries these grasshoppers associate with in their preferred acidic soil habitats.
description: The Huckleberry Spur-throat Grasshopper is a medium-sized hopping insect that's perfectly at home in New England's berry patches and acidic woodlands. Like other spur-throated grasshoppers, it has relatively short antennae (much shorter than its body) and a distinctive pointed projection on its throat that looks like a tiny spur. These grasshoppers typically measure about an inch long and have powerful hind legs built for impressive leaps. Their coloration tends to blend beautifully with dried leaves and berry bushes.

idTips.label: Throat Spur
idTips.description: Look for the small, cone-shaped projection on the throat between the front legs - it feels firm and pointed if you gently touch it with a fingertip, like a tiny thorn

idTips.label: Short Antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are noticeably shorter than the body length and feel thick and sturdy when touched, unlike the thread-like antennae of long-horned grasshoppers

idTips.label: Habitat Association
idTips.description: Almost always found near huckleberry, blueberry, or other low acidic-soil shrubs - if you smell the sweet, slightly tart scent of berry bushes, you're in the right place

idTips.label: Body Coloration
idTips.description: Often has mottled brown and tan coloring that perfectly matches dead huckleberry leaves, with a somewhat rough, textured appearance to the wing covers

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a robust, chunky build and notably muscular hind legs that feel surprisingly strong if you gently hold one

habitat: Look for these grasshoppers in acidic soil areas where huckleberries, blueberries, and other heath family plants thrive - typically forest edges, clearings, and old burns with sandy or peaty soil. They're especially common in areas with scattered low shrubs and partial sunlight, from coastal barrens to mountain slopes up to mid-elevations. The soil in their preferred spots often has that distinctive slightly sour smell of decomposing acidic leaf litter.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are developing in the soil among the berry bush roots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are most easily spotted hopping among huckleberry bushes and calling during warm afternoons and evenings.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with mating and egg-laying occurring before the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off; eggs overwinter in the soil and will hatch the following spring.

funFact: These grasshoppers are essentially living pH test strips - if you find a thriving population of Huckleberry Spur-throats, you can be confident the soil is acidic enough to successfully grow blueberries, azaleas, and other acid-loving plants without any soil amendments!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Melanoplus grasshoppers, but the habitat is your best clue - if it's not in or very near acidic-soil berry bushes, it's probably a different species. Remember: 'Huckleberry hoppers hang around huckleberries' - the habitat association is stronger in this species than most other grasshoppers.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'locust' in 'huckleberry locust' is a common naming confusion - these are true grasshoppers, not the cicadas that are sometimes called locusts, nor the swarming migratory locusts of other continents. In New England, when someone says 'locust,' they might mean grasshoppers, cicadas, or even locust trees!
compareHints: Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Huckleberry Spur-throat is most reliably separated by habitat - Red-legged Grasshoppers prefer more open grassy areas, Two-striped Grasshoppers like agricultural fields, and Pine tree Spur-throats stick to coniferous areas. While many spur-throats are habitat generalists, the Huckleberry species is notably picky about its acidic, berry-bush environment.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Melanoplus relatives in New England, the two-striped grasshopper is the only one with those distinctive twin pale stripes running down its back.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Pine Tree Spur-throat stands out for its strong association with coniferous trees, while most others prefer grasses and herbs in open meadows.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the red-legged grasshopper is distinguished primarily by those characteristic red-orange hind legs, while the two-striped grasshopper has prominent light stripes down its back, and the differential grasshopper is noticeably larger with chevron markings on its hind legs.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the differential grasshopper is distinguished by its larger, more robust build and those characteristic dark leg markings.
